docs.title: GitHub Workshop
docs.text:
This beginner-friendly GitHub workshop was created by SSTIA. It has two parts: first, you will explore GitHub and the open-source community while learning how to find, evaluate, and download repositories; then, you will create and maintain a repository and experience the complete open-source collaboration workflow.

By the end of the workshop, you will be able to:

  • Find open-source projects and decide whether they are suitable for use;
  • Create repositories and use Git to commit and push code;
  • Collaborate through Forks, Issues, and Pull Requests;
  • Write a README, choose an open-source license, and publish a website with GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Towards GitHub
docs.text:
GitHub Logo

GitHub is the world's largest code hosting and collaboration platform, and the gateway to the open-source world for most developers. In this part, you will learn what GitHub and open-source platforms are, register your own account, and learn how to search for, evaluate, and download repositories on GitHub.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• a computer with a browser and internet access;
  • an email address you can check (needed to register a GitHub account);
  • about 30 minutes for this part, plus 60 minutes for the next one.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• What is GitHub: the relationship between GitHub and Git, and the surprising things you can find on GitHub.
  • Open-source platforms: what open-source platforms are, and why GitHub stands out among them.
  • Register a GitHub account: a hands-on exercise — create your own GitHub account step by step.
  • Searching on GitHub: find useful repositories and evaluate them with common metrics.
  • Determine a repository's status: use Insights to tell whether a project is still actively maintained.
  • Download source code: download a ZIP, clone with Git, or grab a release package.
  • Useful repositories: a curated list of repositories worth exploring, with a hands-on exercise.

Some screenshots in this part come from GitHub Docs, used under CC BY 4.0. Image sources.

docs.title: How to Download a Repository's Source Code
docs.text:
There are several common methods. Choose one based on your needs:

Official GitHub Docs screenshots below illustrate the interface; dates, counts, and layout may differ from the current site.

Method 1: Download a ZIP file directly (the simplest option, suitable if you only want to view the code)

Tip

This is suitable when you only want to use a repository's functionality without looking into its source code.

  1. Open the repository page and click the green Code button.
  2. Select Download ZIP from the drop-down menu.
  3. Extract the archive to obtain the complete source code from the repository's current default branch.

Disadvantage: It does not include Git history and cannot pull future updates, so it is suitable for obtaining the code only once.

Method 2: git clone (recommended if you want to use or further develop the code)

The drop-down menu also lets you switch branch or tag first — handy when the version you want is not the default branch.

After installing Git on your computer, open a terminal and run:

Bash
git clone https://github.com/<username>/<repository-name>.git

For example, clone a repository commonly used as an example in this project:

Bash
git clone https://github.com/github/gitignore.git

After cloning, you will have the complete repository and its version history locally. You can later use git pull to retrieve updates from the remote repository.

  • HTTPS (https://github.com/...): Easy to configure and broadly compatible; recommended for beginners.
  • SSH (git@github.com:...): Requires configuring an SSH key first. It is faster and suitable for frequent pushes, but the setup is slightly more complex.

Clone only the latest snapshot

Some repositories have years of history and take a long time to download. git clone --depth 1 downloads only the latest version, which is much faster if you don't need the full history.

Method 3: Download a Release (suitable for software that can be run directly)

If you only want an executable file or installer for a piece of software, do not download the source code. Instead, open the Releases page and download the release package for your platform (Windows / macOS / Linux), such as an .exe, .dmg, or .zip file.

Release pages usually come with release notes describing what changed — read them to decide whether to upgrade.

docs.title: What Is an Open-Source Platform?
docs.text:
An open-source platform is a data hosting platform where source code is made public. It typically hosts a variety of open-source projects.

Open-source platforms usually use licenses to prevent the misuse of open-source content.

Why does open source matter? Because the code is public, anyone can learn from it, reuse it, fix it, and build on it — the software world we use every day is largely built this way. If you want to know how licenses work, see Choose a license in the next part.

Open source is everywhere: the Linux kernel, the Android system, the Chromium browser, Python itself, and the LLaMA models are all open source — reading their code on platforms like GitHub is one of the best ways to learn programming.

docs.title: Well-known (or useful) open-source platforms
docs.text:
• GitHub — the world's largest open-source community platform with the strongest ecosystem.

  • Gitee — a viable domestic alternative to GitHub in China.

  • Hugging Face — an open-source platform for AI models.

docs.title: What platforms are available, and what are GitHub's advantages?
docs.text:
Common code hosting / open-source platforms:

Platform Features GitHub The world's largest and most active community, with the most comprehensive ecosystem GitLab Offers self-hosting (deploying it yourself) and strong integrated DevOps capabilities Bitbucket Developed by Atlassian and integrates well with Jira and other tools Gitee A Chinese platform with fast access and a Chinese-language community SourceForge A long-established open-source project hosting platform GitCode A relatively new code hosting platform in China

GitHub's core advantages:

  1. The largest community: Nearly all well-known open-source projects (such as Linux-related resources, VS Code, React, Vue, and TensorFlow) are hosted on GitHub, where developers, organizations, and companies are highly concentrated.
  2. "Social Coding": Features such as Stars, Forks, Follows, and PRs make both code and developers discoverable and open to collaboration.
  3. The richest ecosystem: GitHub Actions (automation), GitHub Pages (free website hosting), GitHub Copilot (an AI coding assistant), Codespaces, and other supporting services are all readily available.
  4. Generous free tier: A free personal account can create unlimited public repositories (private repositories also have usage limits), which is sufficient for personal learning and small teams.
  5. The de facto standard: The combination of git and GitHub has effectively become an industry-standard workflow. Job hunting, contributing to open source, and reading high-quality source code often begin with GitHub.

docs.title: Practice: Register a GitHub Account
docs.text:
Goal: Have your own GitHub account and be able to sign in and create repositories.

Steps:

  1. Open a browser and visit https://github.com.
  2. Click Sign up in the upper-right corner.
  3. Follow the prompts and enter:
  4. Email: Use an email address that you check regularly and can keep using long-term;
  5. Password: Use at least 8 characters; a combination of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols is recommended;
  6. Username: This will appear in your profile URL, https://github.com/<username>. Choose a short, recognizable, and professional name, such as the pinyin spelling of your name or a commonly used nickname;
  7. Click Create account. GitHub will send a verification email to the address you provided.
  8. Open your email and click Verify email address to complete verification.
  9. Return to GitHub to access your profile page.

docs.title: Recommendations after registration
docs.text:
• Choose your username carefully: it appears in your profile URL, and it is not easy to change later.
  • Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) in Settings → Password and authentication to protect your account.
  • When you enable 2FA, GitHub gives you recovery codes — save them somewhere safe (e.g., a password manager); they are the only way back in if you lose your phone.

Configure SSH so that you can clone GitHub repositories with Git conveniently:

  1. Open a terminal on your computer and generate an SSH key pair (you can accept the default location; a passphrase is optional):

    Bash
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

  2. Display the public key:

    Bash
    cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

  3. Copy the output, go to GitHub Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, paste it, and click Add SSH key.

After that, you can clone repositories using the SSH address (git@github.com:...), which is faster and better for frequent pushes. See Download source code for the difference between HTTPS and SSH.

Student benefits

Registering is also the first step to the GitHub Student Developer Pack — apply with your school email to get GitHub Pro, GitHub Copilot, and dozens of other tools for free.

docs.title: How to Determine a Repository's Current Status
docs.text:
"Status" mainly refers to whether a project is currently active, maintained, or abandoned. You can determine this by reviewing the content under Insights:

Official GitHub Docs screenshots below illustrate the interface; dates, counts, and layout may differ from the current site.

1. Pulse: Check whether the repository has been maintained recently

Pulse summarizes recent Pull Requests, Issues, and commit activity in the repository. If people are still regularly submitting code and handling issues, the project is usually still actively maintained.

2. Check Contributors

The Contributors page shows the number of participants and their contribution trends. If there are many contributors and people are still contributing recently, the project's collaboration and maintenance are relatively healthy.

3. Check commits

Review the date of the most recent commit and the commit frequency to determine whether the code is still being updated. A long period without new commits may mean that the project is stable, or it may mean that maintenance has stopped; check Issues and Releases as well.

4. Check Network

The Network graph shows commit relationships and branch changes between the repository and its forks. If the original repository has stopped updating but one of its forks remains actively developed, you can follow that fork instead.

5. Check Community standards

The Community page shows whether the project provides a contributing guide, a code of conduct, and issue/PR templates. Healthy projects usually take these seriously — it also means they welcome new contributors.

One more sign: the Archived badge

If a repository is archived, GitHub shows an "Archived" banner and makes it read-only: you can still read and fork the code, but no one can push commits or open issues. An archived repository is officially no longer maintained.

Practice: pick a repository you are interested in and use the methods above to judge whether it is still actively maintained — and briefly explain why.

docs.title: Searching on GitHub
docs.text:
Warning

The search bar is at the top; the largest input box is not the search bar.

Tip

So what is that largest input box? It is actually GitHub Copilot, where you can use a variety of advanced models (provided, of course, that you pay).

Official GitHub Docs screenshots below illustrate the interface; dates, counts, and layout may differ from the current site.

Narrow down results with search qualifiers

You can also search with qualifiers, for example stars:>1000 language:python topic:machine-learning returns popular Python repositories about machine learning. GitHub offers many such qualifiers — type your keyword first, then use the sidebar filters or the autocomplete suggestions.

Common qualifiers:

Qualifier Example Meaning stars: stars:>1000 Repositories with more than 1000 stars language: language:python Repositories written in the given language topic: topic:machine-learning Repositories tagged with the given topic user: user:torvalds Repositories owned by the given user org: org:github Repositories owned by the given organization repo: repo:torvalds/linux Restrict the search to the given repository pushed: pushed:>2026-01-01 Repositories pushed to recently (still alive?)

Note

Two more things to know: code search requires signing in to GitHub, and results can be sorted by Best match, Most stars, or Recently updated using the sort menu above the result list.

docs.title: How to evaluate a repository
docs.text:
When you encounter an unfamiliar repository, you can quickly assess whether it is worth using, learning from, or contributing to based on the following dimensions:

Dimension Where to Look Description Stars ⭐ in the upper-right corner of the repository page Similar to favorites/likes and the most visible indicator of popularity; generally, more is better Forks Next to Stars The number of times the repository has been copied for further development, indicating how many people have built upon it Watchers Repository page The number of people following the repository, indicating sustained interest Issues Issues tab Check the number of issues and whether maintainers respond to and resolve them promptly; see Report problems with issues Latest commit time File list / Commits Indicates whether the project is still being maintained Number of contributors Insights → Contributors More contributors generally indicate healthier collaboration License Repository root / About section on the right Determines whether and how you may use the code README quality Repository home page Check whether it provides clear introductions, installation instructions, and usage guidance Releases / Tags Releases tab Check whether stable versions exist and how frequently new versions are released

docs.title: Some Useful Repositories
docs.text:
The following public repositories are very useful for learning and getting started. Search for and explore them according to your interests:

Besides this list, GitHub Explore and GitHub Trending are two good places to discover new projects every day.

Learning

  • free-programming-books-zh: A collection of free Chinese programming books.
  • freeCodeCamp/freeCodeCamp: An open-source platform offering free programming courses and exercises.
  • TheAlgorithms: A collection of data structures and algorithms implemented in various programming languages.
  • build-your-own-x: Implement things from scratch (databases, operating systems, compilers, ...) in your favorite language.
  • every-programmer-should-know: A curated list of things every programmer should know.

Resource Collections (Awesome Lists)

  • awesome: A central collection of curated resource lists covering a wide variety of topics.
  • awesome-chinese / various awesome-xxx repositories: Curated resource lists organized by topic, making it easy to follow a trail of useful resources.

Engineering / Tools

  • github/gitignore: A collection of .gitignore templates for various languages and environments.
  • microsoft/vscode: The source code of Microsoft's open-source editor, VS Code; suitable for studying a large-scale project.
  • vuejs/vue and facebook/react: The source code of mainstream front-end frameworks.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
1. Search for a topic that interests you.
  2. Find a well-maintained repository.
  3. Download some useful code.

docs.title: What Is GitHub?
docs.text:
GitHub is a code hosting and collaboration platform built on the Git version control system. It launched in 2008 and was acquired by Microsoft in 2018. Simply put, it is a website for "storing code and writing code with others."

Today it has more than 100 million registered developers, and most of the open-source projects you will meet in your courses are hosted here.

Tip

GitHub is different from Git. GitHub is an open-source platform whose repositories are based on Git. You can also find unexpected things on GitHub, even if they have nothing to do with coding. In theory, you can upload anything you want to share.

docs.title: Git, the engine behind GitHub
docs.text:
Git is a distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds in 2005. It runs on your own computer and records every change you make to your files. Thanks to Git, you can:

  • go back to any previous version at any time (no more homework_final_v2_really_final.zip);
  • work in parallel with others through branches, and merge your work back together.

A few terms you will meet again and again:

Term Meaning Repository (仓库) The place where a project's files and history live Commit (提交) A snapshot of your changes, like a save point in a game Branch (分支) A parallel line of development; the default branch is usually called main Remote (远端) A copy of the repository hosted on a server, such as GitHub

GitHub builds on Git: it hosts the remote repositories, and adds the web interface and the community features you will see throughout this workshop.

docs.title: Some interesting examples
docs.text:
• Free Programming Books: A community-maintained collection of free programming books and learning resources.

  • HowToCook: A programmer's guide to cooking at home, with clear, step-by-step recipes.

  • No Code: A humorous project about writing no code and deploying nowhere. This popular "empty repository" still contains a README and other files.

  • 科技爱好者周刊 (Tech Enthusiast Weekly): A weekly technology newsletter that welcomes reader submissions through Issues.

  • OSSU Computer Science: A community-organized curriculum for teaching yourself computer science.

docs.title: Beyond code hosting
docs.text: In addition to hosting code, GitHub also provides features such as Issues (issue tracking), Actions (automation), Pages (static website hosting), Wiki (documentation), and Codespaces (cloud development environments). It has evolved into a complete developer community and engineering collaboration ecosystem.

docs.title: Documentations
docs.text: Official documentation and recommended reading if you want to go deeper after the workshop:

docs.title: Official documentation
docs.text: • GitHub Docs — the official documentation maintained by GitHub, covering everything from repositories and pull requests to Actions and the API.

docs.title: Recommended reading
docs.text:
• GitHub 漫游指南 — a Chinese ebook on how to build a good project on GitHub. It explores how users behave on GitHub and shares many interesting observations.
  • Pro Git — the classic free book on Git, from the basics to the internals.
  • GitHub Skills — free interactive courses that teach Git and GitHub by doing, right inside a repository.

docs.title: Fancy Videos
docs.text: Some fun and instructive videos about Git, GitHub, and working with others — enjoy them, and learn from other people's (mis)adventures.

Using a GitHub Repository
docs.text:
Author: Zhang Junming

In the first part, you learned what GitHub is and how to find, evaluate, and download repositories. Now it is time to create your own repository and maintain it, and to experience the complete open-source collaboration workflow.

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • a GitHub account (see Register a GitHub account);
  • Git installed on your computer, and a terminal you are comfortable with.

docs.title: The overall workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Create a repository] --> B[Choose a license and write a README]
    B --> C[Edit files and commit]
    C --> D[Open an issue before contributing]
    D --> E[Fork others' repositories and send pull requests]
    E --> F[Publish your project with GitHub Pages]

In a nutshell:

First create a repository → use a license and a README to clarify the project → open an issue before contributing → fork and follow the pull request flow → use web editing for small daily changes → once the project matures, publish a web page for display.

docs.title: By the end of this part
docs.text:
You will have:

  • a repository of your own, with a license and a README;
  • your own web page published with GitHub Pages;
  • a fork of someone else's repository (and maybe a pull request to it);
  • a well-written issue you have opened.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
• Create a repository: create your first repository and put code into it.
  • Choose a license: decide how others may use your code.
  • Report problems with issues: the built-in ticket system of a repository, and the first step of contributing.
  • Fork a repository: copy someone else's repository to your own account.
  • Contribute with a pull request: the core flow of open-source collaboration.
  • Edit files on the web: make quick changes without local Git.
  • Write a README: the "first business card" of your project.
  • Publish with GitHub Pages: turn your repository into a free website.

docs.title: How to Contribute to a Repository
docs.text:
The core process of contributing is Issue → Fork → Modify → Pull Request (PR).

Start with an issue and only write code after you reach agreement with the maintainer: this avoids duplicated work (someone may already be fixing it) and misunderstandings (the maintainer may not want that feature at all).

  1. Open an issue to report the bug or propose the feature, and discuss it with the maintainer (see Report problems with issues). If someone else already reported it, join that discussion — and mention that you would like to fix it.

  2. Fork the target repository (see Fork a repository) and clone your fork locally:

    Bash
    git clone https://github.com/your-username/repository-name.git
cd repository-name

  3. Create a new branch to avoid modifying main directly:

    Bash
    git checkout -b <branch name>

  4. Modify the code or documentation, then commit (I believe you are already very familiar with these from 151 or 101):

    Bash
    git add .
git commit -m "Describe your changes"
git push origin <branch name>

    Don't force-add ignored files

    Suppose your .gitignore ignores .o files, but you still run:

    Bash
    git add -f main.o

    This will force the addition and treat main.o as a tracked file, so try not to write -f.

  5. Go back to your fork page on GitHub and click Contribute → Open pull request.

  6. Clearly describe what you changed and why (be detailed) — a good description explains what problem you solve, how you solve it, and how the change can be tested. Mention the related issue (e.g., fixes #12) to link them together, then click Create pull request.
  7. Wait for the original repository maintainer to review; they may give feedback, and you can continue to modify and push to update the same PR.

Supplements:

  • If you just find a bug or want to make a suggestion, you can directly submit a New issue on the repository's Issues page. This is also a way to contribute — see Report problems with issues for how to write a good one.
  • If the original repository gives you write permission, you can skip the fork and directly create a branch, make changes, and submit a PR.
  • New to open source? Search for issues labeled good first issue — maintainers use this label to mark beginner-friendly tasks.
  • Keep a pull request small and focused — one PR solves one problem; it is much easier to review and merge.
  • Work in progress? Open a draft pull request so the maintainer knows not to review it yet.
  • After your PR is merged, you can safely delete your feature branch.

  • If the original repository keeps updating, sync your fork from time to time:

    Bash
    git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/repository-name.git
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

docs.title: How to Create a Repository
docs.text:
A repository (repo for short) is where a project's files live on GitHub, and the basic unit of code hosting and collaboration. Every project starts with creating one.

  1. Log in to github.com, click the + icon in the upper right corner, and select New repository.
  2. Fill in the information:
  3. Repository name: Required, e.g., my-first-project.
  4. Description: Optional, a brief explanation of what the repository is for.
  5. Public / Private: A public repository can be viewed by anyone; a private repository can only be viewed by you and invited people.
  6. Add a README file: Recommended, automatically generates a README.md.
  7. Add .gitignore: Optional, ignores files that don't need to be uploaded based on your language (C/C++, Python, etc.).
  8. Choose a license: Optional, select an open-source license (see Choose a license).
  9. Click Create repository to finish creating.

Naming and visibility

  • Name your repository with lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens (e.g., my-first-project), so the URL stays clean.
  • You can change Public / Private later in Settings → General, so don't stress about it now.
  • The .gitignore file tells Git which files not to track (build outputs, IDE files, secrets); you can start from the language template GitHub provides.

Renaming and the default branch

  • You can rename a repository later in Settings → General, but the old URL stops working for everyone (GitHub redirects visitors, so try not to rename once people link to it).
  • Since October 2020, new repositories use main as the default branch name (some older tutorials may still say master).

docs.title: Put code into the repository
docs.text:
After creating it, you have two ways to put code into the repository:

  • Web operations: Click Add file → Upload files to drag and drop directly.
  • Local Git: Copy the repository address and run in the terminal:
Bash
git clone https://github.com/your-username/repository-name.git
# After placing files inside
git add .
git commit -m "first commit"
git push

First-time Git configuration

If your computer has not been configured with a username and email, you cannot commit. Configure them as follows (if you don't want a global configuration and only want to configure this one repository, remove --global):

Bash
git config --global user.name <your name, come up with one yourself>
git config --global user.email <email>
git config --list # used to confirm your configuration status

docs.title: How to Quickly Edit Content in a Repository
docs.text:
You don't need local Git; you can quickly edit directly on the web page:

  1. Open a file in the repository and click the pencil icon (Edit this file) in the upper right corner.
  2. Modify the content directly in the edit box.
  3. Scroll to the bottom of the page, write a short commit message, and choose to commit to the current branch or a new branch.
  4. Click Commit changes to save.

Other web shortcuts:

  • New file: Add file → Create new file.
  • Upload file: Add file → Upload files.
  • Delete file: Open the file → trash can icon in the upper right corner → Commit.

Note

Web editing is suitable for small changes (changing documentation, fixing one line of code). For large changes that require local compilation and testing, the local Git workflow in Contribute with a pull request is still more suitable.

Even faster: the web editor

On any repository page, press the . (period) key to open the repository in github.dev, a full VS Code editor running in your browser. It is very handy for browsing or editing code without cloning.

Edit and propose changes in one go

When committing a web edit, you can choose Create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request — GitHub then opens a pull request for you directly. This is a very common way to contribute small fixes to other people's repositories.

docs.title: How to Fork a Repository
docs.text:
Fork means completely copying someone else's repository to your own account, after which you can modify it freely without affecting the original repository.

  1. Open the repository page you want to fork.
  2. Click the Fork button in the upper right corner (usually next to Star).
  3. Select the target account (usually yourself) and click Create fork.
  4. After completion, a repository with the same name will appear under your account, marked "forked from original author/original repository".

After getting the fork, clone it locally:

Bash
git clone https://github.com/your-username/repository-name.git

Fork vs. clone

A fork happens on GitHub: the entire repository is copied to your own account as a new remote repository. git clone downloads a repository to your local computer. To work on a fork, you usually do both: fork first, then clone your fork.

A quick comparison of the three buttons you see on every repository page:

Action What it does Typical use Star ⭐ Bookmarks the repository for you Save it for later; also a sign of appreciation Watch 👁 Subscribes to notifications Follow a project's new releases and discussions Fork Copies the repository into your account Modify the code or prepare a pull request

Uses: wanting to do secondary development based on someone else's project, learn the source code, or prepare to submit a Pull Request to the original project (see Contribute with a pull request). If you plan to contribute a fix, discuss it in an issue first — see Report problems with issues.

A fork does not sync itself

Your fork is a snapshot of the repository at the moment you forked it. When the original repository updates, your fork does not follow automatically — see Contribute with a pull request for how to sync it via upstream. Also note that anyone can fork a public repository freely, while private repositories cannot be forked by others.

docs.title: How to Publish a Website with GitHub Pages
docs.text:
GitHub Pages can turn a repository into a free hosted static website.

  1. Open the repository → Settings → Pages on the left.
  2. Under Build and deployment, select Deploy from a branch for Source.
  3. Select the branch (usually main) and directory (root directory / or /docs), and click Save.
  4. After a few dozen seconds, the page will give you your URL: https://your-username.github.io/repository-name/.

Content sources:

  • The simplest approach: Place an index.html in the repository root directory; this is the homepage.
  • You can also use Jekyll (built into GitHub) to automatically generate blog-style pages by selecting a theme.
  • There is also a "user homepage" type: Create a repository named your-username.github.io, and the URL will be https://your-username.github.io/.

Tip

If you are not satisfied with plain HTML, you can generate a static site from Markdown with tools like MkDocs (which builds this very workshop website) or Hugo, and publish the result to GitHub Pages in the same way.

Troubleshooting:

  • The first deployment takes about a minute; you can watch the progress in the Actions tab of your repository.
  • If the site returns 404, check that Source is set to Deploy from a branch and that the correct branch and directory are selected.
  • After you push new commits to the selected branch, GitHub Pages rebuilds the site automatically.

Two things to remember

  • Public repositories only: on a free account, GitHub Pages can only be published from public repositories (private repositories require GitHub Pro).
  • Custom domain: in Settings → Pages, you can bind your own domain name, and GitHub will issue a free HTTPS certificate for it.

docs.title: How to Use Issues
docs.text:
An Issue is GitHub's built-in ticket system. Anyone can use it to:

  • report a bug;
  • request a feature;
  • ask a question;
  • track a task (some teams plan their whole project in issues).

An issue is not a private message to the maintainer: it is public, searchable, and becomes part of the repository's history — which is why writing it well matters.

It is also the recommended first step before writing any code for someone else's project: discuss first, then contribute (see Contribute with a pull request).

docs.title: How to open an issue
docs.text:
1. Open the repository and go to the Issues tab, then click New issue.
  2. If the repository provides issue templates (e.g., "Bug report", "Feature request"), choose the matching one — it will guide you through the form.
  3. Write a clear title that summarizes the problem, e.g., App crashes when opening a .png file on Windows.
  4. Describe it in detail (see the checklist below) and click Submit new issue.

docs.title: What a good issue looks like
docs.text:
• Search first: your problem may already be reported — comment on the existing issue instead of duplicating it.
  • One issue, one problem: don't bundle several unrelated problems together.
  • Clear title: the title alone should tell the maintainer what it is about.
  • Steps to reproduce: what you did, step by step, and what happened.
  • Expected vs. actual behavior: what you expected to happen, and what actually happened.
  • Environment: operating system, software version, programming language version, etc.
  • Evidence: screenshots, error messages, or log excerpts (wrap logs in a code block).

docs.title: How an issue lives
docs.text:
• Labels: maintainers tag issues with labels such as bug, enhancement, question, or good first issue (beginner-friendly tasks — see Contribute with a pull request).
  • Mentioning people: write @username in the issue body to notify a specific person.
  • Closing: the maintainer closes the issue when it is resolved. If a commit or pull request description contains fixes #<issue number>, GitHub closes the issue automatically when that commit or PR is merged.
  • Discussions: some projects prefer GitHub Discussions for Q&A — check whether the repository has a Discussions tab before asking a question in an issue.

Tip

Opening a well-written issue is itself a contribution to open source: it helps maintainers and other users alike. Don't be afraid to report problems — just describe them carefully.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
1. Open an issue in your own repository (e.g., describe a feature you plan to add) and close it yourself.
  2. Go to a repository you often use and find an issue labeled good first issue — read it and think about whether you could solve it.

docs.title: What Is a License?
docs.text:
A License is a legal statement that specifies how others may use your code. It is an important part of open-source projects:

License Features Applicable Scenarios MIT The most permissive; others can use, modify, and commercialize freely, only needing to retain the copyright notice Most personal projects Apache 2.0 Permissive + explicit patent grant Enterprises, needing patent protection GPL Strong "infectiousness"; if you use it, you must also open-source Want derivative projects to be open-source too BSD Similar to MIT, with slightly more clauses Academic projects Unlicense Waives all rights; the code enters the public domain Want zero restrictions at all

Key points:

  • No license means "all rights reserved" by default; others cannot legally copy or modify your code.
  • How to add: Select it directly when creating the repository, or later click Add file → Create new file, write the file name as LICENSE.txt, and GitHub will automatically provide template options.
  • When GitHub generates the license file from a template, it inserts a placeholder copyright line ([year] [fullname]) — remember to replace it with your own name and the current year.

Tip

Not sure which license to choose? choosealicense.com is maintained by GitHub — answer a few simple questions and it will recommend a suitable license for your project.

Which one should I pick?

If in doubt: MIT for personal and course projects, Apache 2.0 if you care about patents, GPL if you want derivatives to stay open. You can also change the license later by replacing the LICENSE file (for serious projects with many contributors, everyone should agree first).

docs.title: How to Write a README
docs.text:
README.md is the documentation displayed by default on the homepage after opening the repository, written in Markdown. It is the "first business card" for others to understand your project.

A good README usually includes:

  • Project introduction: One sentence explaining what this project does.
  • Installation method: Environment dependencies, how to install.
  • Usage method: How to run, example code.
  • License / Contribution method: Point to LICENSE or explain how to participate.

docs.title: Common Markdown syntax
docs.text:
Markdown
# Level 1 heading
## Level 2 heading
- List item
**Bold**, *italic*
`inline code`
[link text](URL)
![image description](image URL)
```
code block
```

A few more pieces that are commonly used:

Markdown
| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| cell | cell |

- [x] done task
- [ ] todo task

> quote

How to create: Check "Add a README file" when creating a new repository, or later click Add file → Create new file and write the file name as README.md.

docs.title: A simple README skeleton
docs.text:
You can start from this outline and fill in your own content:

Markdown
# Project name

One sentence: what does this project do?

## Installation

How to install dependencies and set things up.

## Usage

How to run it, with an example command.

## Contributing

How others can participate, and a link to the license.

Images and badges

  • To use images, put them in the repository (e.g., in an images/ folder) and reference them with relative paths; or drag an image into an issue comment and copy the generated URL.
  • One-line status badges from shields.io (build status, license, downloads, ...) make a README look professional.

docs.title: GitHub Workshop
docs.text:
这是一个由 SSTIA 制作、面向初学者的 GitHub 入门 Workshop。课程分为两部分：先认识 GitHub 与开源社区，学习搜索、判断和下载仓库；再动手创建和维护仓库，体验完整的开源协作流程。

完成课程后，你将能够：

  • 查找并判断一个开源项目是否值得使用；
  • 创建仓库，使用 Git 提交和推送代码；
  • 通过 Fork、Issue 和 Pull Request 参与协作；
  • 编写 README、选择开源许可证，并用 GitHub Pages 发布网站。

docs.title: 走近 GitHub
docs.text:
GitHub Logo: Octocat

GitHub 是全球最大的代码托管与协作平台，也是大多数开发者进入开源世界的入口。在本部分中，你将了解 GitHub 与开源平台是什么，注册自己的账号，并学会如何在 GitHub 上搜索、判断和下载仓库。

docs.title: 开始之前
docs.text:
• 一台能上网的电脑和浏览器；
  • 一个能正常收信的邮箱（注册 GitHub 账号要用）；
  • 本章节大约需要 30 分钟，下一章节大约需要 60 分钟。

docs.title: 你将学到
docs.text:
• GitHub 是什么：GitHub 与 Git 的关系，以及你能在 GitHub 上找到的意想不到的内容。
  • 开源平台：开源平台是什么，以及 GitHub 在其中有什么优势。
  • 注册 GitHub 账号：动手实践，一步步创建自己的账号。
  • 在 GitHub 上搜索：找到有用的仓库，并用常用指标评估它们。
  • 判断仓库的维护状态：用 Insights 判断一个项目是否仍在活跃维护。
  • 下载源代码：下载 ZIP、用 Git 克隆，或者下载发行版。
  • 一些有用的仓库：一份值得探索的仓库清单，并附实践环节。

本部分部分截图来自 GitHub Docs，依据 CC BY 4.0 使用。图片来源。

docs.title: 怎么下载一个仓库的源代码
docs.text:
有几种常用方式，按场景选择：

下方 GitHub 官方文档截图用于展示界面；日期、数量和布局可能与当前网站有所不同。

方式一：直接下载 ZIP（最简单，适合只想看代码）

Tip

这适用于你只想使用某个仓库的功能而不想知道它的源代码具体长什么样的时候

  1. 进入仓库主页，点击绿色的 Code 按钮。
  2. 在下拉菜单中选择 Download ZIP。
  3. 解压后即可得到该仓库当前默认分支的完整源代码。

缺点：不含 Git 历史记录，也无法后续拉取更新，适合一次性获取代码。

方式二：git clone（推荐，适合要使用/二次开发）

下拉菜单里还可以先切换分支或标签（tag）——当你要的不是默认分支的版本时非常有用。

在电脑上安装 Git 后，打开终端（Terminal），执行：

Bash
git clone https://github.com/<用户名>/<仓库名>.git

例如克隆本项目常用的示例：

Bash
git clone https://github.com/github/gitignore.git

克隆完成后，本地就拥有该仓库的完整内容与版本历史，之后可用 git pull 获取远端更新。

  • HTTPS 方式（https://github.com/...）：配置简单，通用性最好，推荐初学者使用。
  • SSH 方式（git@github.com:...）：需要先配置 SSH 密钥，速度更快、适合频繁推送，但配置稍复杂。

只想快速拿到最新代码？

有些仓库历史很长、体积很大，完整克隆会很久。git clone --depth 1 只下载最新版本，速度快很多，适合不需要完整历史记录的场景。

方式三：下载 Release 发行版（适合下载可直接运行的软件）

如果只是想下载某个软件的可执行文件或安装包，不要下载源码，而是进入 Releases 页面，下载对应平台（Windows / macOS / Linux）的 .exe、.dmg、.zip 等发行包。

发行页面通常会附带更新说明（Release notes），可以看看都改了什么再决定是否升级。

docs.title: 什么是开源平台
docs.text:
开源平台，即是公开源代码的数据托管平台，通常承载了各种不同的开源项目。

开源平台通常会设置许可证，避免开源内容滥用。

开源为什么重要？因为代码公开，任何人都可以学习它、复用它、修复它、基于它继续开发——我们每天使用的软件世界，很大程度上就是这样建成的。想了解许可证如何运作，可以看下一部分的 选择许可证。

开源其实无处不在：Linux 内核、Android 系统、Chromium 浏览器、Python 语言本身、LLaMA 模型……都是开源项目。在 GitHub 这样的平台上阅读它们的源码，是学习编程最好的方式之一。

docs.title: 经典（或者有用）的开源平台
docs.text:
• GitHub——目前世界上最大、生态最好的开源社区平台。

  • Gitee——国内一个可行的 GitHub 替代平台。

  • Hugging Face——AI 模型的开源平台。

docs.title: 开源平台有哪些，GitHub 在其中的优势是什么
docs.text:
常见的代码托管 / 开源平台：

平台 特点 GitHub 全球最大、社区最活跃，生态最完善 GitLab 提供自托管（自己部署）方案，DevOps 一体化能力强 Bitbucket 由 Atlassian 出品，与 Jira 等工具集成好 Gitee（码云） 国内平台，访问速度快，中文社区 SourceForge 老牌开源项目托管站 GitCode 国内较新的开源托管平台

GitHub 的核心优势：

  1. 社区规模最大：几乎所有知名开源项目（如 Linux 相关资料、VS Code、React、Vue、TensorFlow 等）都托管在 GitHub 上，开发者、组织和公司高度聚集。
  2. "社交化编程"（Social Coding）：通过 Star（收藏/点赞）、Fork（复刻）、Follow（关注）、PR 等方式，让代码和开发者都"可被发现、可被协作"。
  3. 生态最丰富：GitHub Actions（自动化）、GitHub Pages（免费网站托管）、GitHub Copilot（AI 编程助手）、Codespaces 等配套服务一应俱全。
  4. 免费额度友好：个人免费账号即可创建无限公开仓库（私有仓库也有限额），对个人学习和小型团队足够使用。
  5. 事实上的标准：git + GitHub 的用法几乎成为行业通行做法，找工作、参与开源、阅读优秀源码大多从 GitHub 开始。

docs.title: 实践：注册 GitHub 账号
docs.text:
目标：拥有一个自己的 GitHub 账号，能登录、能创建仓库。

步骤：

  1. 打开浏览器，访问 https://github.com。
  2. 点击右上角 Sign up（注册）。
  3. 按提示依次填写：
  4. 邮箱：建议用常用、可长期使用的邮箱；
  5. 密码：至少 8 位，建议包含大小写字母、数字和符号；
  6. 用户名（Username）：会出现在你的主页地址 https://github.com/<用户名> 中，建议用简短、易识别、专业的名字（如姓名拼音或常用昵称）；
  7. 点击 Create account，GitHub 会向你填写的邮箱发送一封验证邮件。
  8. 登录邮箱，点击邮件中的 Verify email address 完成验证。
  9. 回到 GitHub，即可进入你的个人主页。

docs.title: 完成注册后的建议
docs.text:
• 用户名要慎重选择：它会出现在你的主页地址里，之后并不容易修改。
  • 开启两步验证（2FA）：在 Settings → Password and authentication 中开启，保护账号安全。
  • 开启 2FA 时，GitHub 会给你一串恢复代码（Recovery codes）——请妥善保存（比如放进密码管理器），手机丢失时它们是找回账号的唯一途径。

配置 SSH，便于之后使用 Git 克隆 GitHub 上的仓库：

  1. 在电脑上打开终端，生成一对 SSH 密钥（可以直接使用默认保存位置，密码口令可留空）：

    Bash
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

  2. 查看公钥内容：

    Bash
    cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

  3. 复制输出的内容，进入 GitHub Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key，粘贴后点击 Add SSH key。

配置完成后，就可以使用 SSH 地址（git@github.com:...）克隆仓库，速度更快、更适合频繁推送。HTTPS 与 SSH 的区别见 下载源代码。

学生福利

注册完账号，还可以用学校邮箱申请 GitHub Student Developer Pack，免费获得 GitHub Pro、GitHub Copilot 等权益。

docs.title: 如何判断一个仓库现在的状态
docs.text:
"状态"主要指这个项目目前是活跃、维护中，还是已经弃坑。判断方法：观察 Insights 中的内容。

下方 GitHub 官方文档截图用于展示界面；日期、数量和布局可能与当前网站有所不同。

1. Pulse：检查这个仓库最近是否有人维护

Pulse 会汇总仓库近期的 Pull Request、Issue 和提交活动。若最近持续有人提交代码、处理问题，通常说明项目仍在活跃维护。

2. 看 Contributors

Contributors 页面可以看到参与者数量及各自的贡献趋势。贡献者较多且近期仍有人持续贡献，说明项目的协作和维护相对健康。

3. 看 commits

查看最近一次提交时间以及提交频率，判断代码是否还在更新。长期没有新提交可能表示项目已稳定，也可能已经停止维护，需要结合 Issue 和 Release 一起判断。

4. 看 Network

Network 图展示仓库及其 Fork 之间的提交关系和分支变化。如果原仓库更新停滞，但某个 Fork 仍在活跃开发，可以进一步关注该 Fork。

5. 看 Community 规范

Community 页面会显示项目是否提供贡献指南、行为准则（Code of Conduct）和 Issue/PR 模板。健康维护的项目通常都会认真准备这些——这也说明他们欢迎新贡献者。

还有一个信号：Archived 标记

如果仓库被归档（Archived），GitHub 会在页面上显示 "Archived" 横幅，并把仓库设为只读：你仍然可以查看和 fork 代码，但任何人都无法再提交或提 Issue。被归档意味着官方已经不再维护这个项目。

实践环节： 挑一个你感兴趣的仓库，用上面的方法判断它是否还在活跃维护，并简要说明你的理由。

docs.title: 在 GitHub 上搜索
docs.text:
Warning

搜索栏在上方，那个最大的输入框不是搜索栏

Tip

那么这个最大的输入框是什么？实际上这是 GitHub Copilot，在这里你可以使用许多不同的先进模型（当然，前提是得付费）

下方 GitHub 官方文档截图用于展示界面；日期、数量和布局可能与当前网站有所不同。

用限定符缩小搜索范围

搜索时还可以使用限定符（qualifier），例如 stars:>1000 language:python topic:machine-learning 会返回关于机器学习的、Star 数超过 1000 的 Python 仓库。GitHub 提供了许多这样的限定符——先输入关键词，再使用侧边栏筛选或自动补全建议即可。

常用限定符：

限定符 示例 含义 stars: stars:>1000 Star 数超过 1000 的仓库 language: language:python 使用指定语言编写的仓库 topic: topic:machine-learning 带有指定主题标签的仓库 user: user:torvalds 某个用户名下的仓库 org: org:github 某个组织名下的仓库 repo: repo:torvalds/linux 只在指定仓库内搜索 pushed: pushed:>2026-01-01 最近仍有推送更新的仓库（还活着吗？）

Note

还有两点：代码搜索需要先登录 GitHub 才能使用；结果列表上方有排序菜单，可以按 Best match（最佳匹配）、Most stars（最多 Star）或 Recently updated（最近更新）排序。

docs.title: 怎么评价一个仓库
docs.text:
面对一个陌生仓库，可以从以下几个维度快速评估它"值不值得用 / 学 / 参与"：

维度 在哪里看 说明 Star 数 仓库主页右上角 ⭐ 相当于"收藏/点赞"数，是受欢迎程度最直观的指标，一般越多越好 Fork 数 Star 旁边 被复刻的次数，反映有多少人基于它做二次开发 Watch 数 仓库主页 关注人数，反映持续关注度 Issue 情况 Issues 标签页 看 issue 数量、是否有维护者及时回复和处理；Issue 怎么用见 用 Issue 反馈问题 最近提交时间 文件列表 / Commits 判断项目是否还在维护 Contributor 数量 Insights → Contributors 参与人数越多，说明协作越健康 License 仓库根目录 / 右侧 About 决定你能不能用、怎么用这份代码 README 质量 仓库首页 是否有清晰的介绍、安装和使用说明 Release / Tag Releases 标签页 是否有稳定版本号，是否频繁发版

docs.title: 一些有用的仓库
docs.text:
以下是一些对学习和入门非常有帮助的公开仓库，可按兴趣搜索并实践：

除了这份清单，GitHub Explore 和 GitHub Trending 也是每天发现新项目的好去处。

学习类

  • free-programming-books-zh：免费的中文编程书籍合集。
  • freeCodeCamp/freeCodeCamp：开源的免费编程学习课程与练习平台。
  • TheAlgorithms：用各种语言实现的数据结构与算法合集。
  • build-your-own-x：用你喜欢的语言从零实现各种技术（数据库、操作系统、编译器……）。
  • every-programmer-should-know：每个程序员都应该知道的知识清单。

资源合集类（Awesome 系列）

  • awesome：各种主题的"精选资源清单"总入口。
  • awesome-chinese / 各类 awesome-xxx：按主题整理的优质资源列表，非常适合按图索骥。

工程/工具类

  • github/gitignore：各种语言和环境的 .gitignore 模板合集。
  • microsoft/vscode：微软的开源编辑器 VS Code 源码，适合阅读大型项目。
  • vuejs/vue、facebook/react：主流前端框架源码。

docs.title: 实践环节
docs.text:
1. 搜索一个感兴趣的话题
  2. 找到一个维护良好的仓库
  3. 下载一些有用的代码

docs.title: GitHub 是什么
docs.text:
GitHub 是一个基于 Git 版本控制系统构建的代码托管与协作平台，于 2008 年上线，2018 年被微软收购。简单来说，它是一个"存放代码、和别人一起写代码"的网站。

今天它已经拥有超过 1 亿注册开发者，你在课程中会遇到的绝大多数开源项目都托管在这里。

Tip

GitHub 与 Git 不同。GitHub 是一个开源平台，其仓库基于 Git。不过，你能在 GitHub 上找到一些意想不到的内容，即使它们与编程毫无关系。 理论上，你可以放上任何你想分享的内容。

docs.title: 幕后的 Git
docs.text:
Git 是一个分布式版本控制系统，由 Linus Torvalds 于 2005 年创建。它运行在你自己的电脑上，记录你对文件的每一次改动。有了 Git，你可以：

  • 随时回到任意一个历史版本（再也不需要 作业_最终版_真的最终版.zip 了）；
  • 通过分支（branch）与别人并行开发，最后再把工作合并到一起。

下面几个术语会在后面反复出现：

术语 含义 仓库（Repository） 存放项目文件与历史记录的地方 提交（Commit） 一次改动的快照，就像游戏里的存档点 分支（Branch） 一条并行的开发线，默认分支通常叫 main 远端（Remote） 托管在服务器上的仓库副本，比如 GitHub 上的那份

GitHub 就建立在 Git 之上：它托管远端仓库，并提供了网页界面和本 workshop 中你会看到的种种社区功能。

docs.title: 一些有趣的例子
docs.text:
• Free Programming Books：由社区维护的免费编程书籍和学习资源合集。

  • HowToCook：程序员的居家做饭指南，提供清晰、分步骤的菜谱。

  • No Code：一个以"不写代码，也不部署到任何地方"为主题的幽默项目。这个受欢迎的"空仓库"仍然包含 README 和其他文件。

  • 科技爱好者周刊：每周发布的科技资讯周刊，欢迎读者通过 Issues 投稿。

  • OSSU Computer Science：由社区组织的计算机科学自学课程体系。

docs.title: GitHub 仓库的使用
docs.text:
作者： 张峻铭

在第一部分中，你已经了解了 GitHub 是什么，以及如何搜索、判断和下载仓库。现在轮到你自己动手：创建一个仓库并维护它，体验完整的开源协作流程。

开始之前，请先确认你已经有：

  • 一个 GitHub 账号（见 注册 GitHub 账号）；
  • 电脑上安装好 Git，并且会用终端（Terminal）。

docs.title: 整体流程
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[创建仓库] --> B[选择许可证并编写 README]
    B --> C[编辑文件并提交]
    C --> D[参与贡献前先开 Issue 沟通]
    D --> E[Fork 别人的仓库并发起 Pull Request]
    E --> F[用 GitHub Pages 发布项目网页]

一句话总结：

先用创建仓库建仓库 → 用许可证和 README 把项目弄清楚 → 参与贡献前先开 Issue 沟通 → Fork 之后走 Pull Request 流程 → 平时小改动在网页上编辑 → 项目成熟后用 GitHub Pages 搭个网页展示。

docs.title: 完成本部分后
docs.text:
你将拥有：

  • 一个属于自己的仓库，带许可证和 README；
  • 一个用 GitHub Pages 发布的网页；
  • 一个别人仓库的 fork（说不定还向它发起了 Pull Request）；
  • 一份你自己提交的、写得很清楚的 Issue。

docs.title: 章节
docs.text:
• 创建仓库：创建你的第一个仓库，并把代码放进去。
  • 选择许可证：决定别人可以怎样使用你的代码。
  • 用 Issue 反馈问题：仓库内置的"工单系统"，也是参与贡献的第一步。
  • Fork 一个仓库：把别人的仓库复制到你自己的账号下。
  • 通过 Pull Request 参与贡献：开源协作的核心流程。
  • 在网页上快速编辑：不需要本地 Git 的小改动。
  • 编写 README：你项目的"第一张名片"。
  • 用 GitHub Pages 发布网页：把仓库变成一个免费网站。

docs.title: 通过 Pull Request 参与贡献
如何参与贡献
docs.text:
贡献的核心流程是 Issue → Fork → 修改 → Pull Request（PR）。

先开 Issue 沟通、达成一致后再动手写代码：这样既不会重复劳动（别人可能已经在修了），也不会白费力气（维护者可能根本不想要这个功能）。

  1. 先开 Issue 报告 bug 或提出功能设想，并和维护者讨论（见 用 Issue 反馈问题）。如果已经有人提过，就在那个 Issue 下参与讨论——并说明你想来修它。

  2. Fork 目标仓库（见 Fork 一个仓库），并克隆自己的 fork 到本地：

    Bash
    git clone https://github.com/你的用户名/仓库名.git
cd 仓库名

  3. 新建一个分支，避免直接在 main 上改：

    Bash
    git checkout -b <分支名>

  4. 修改代码或文档，然后提交（相信这些在 151 or 101 已经很熟练了）：

    Bash
    git add .
git commit -m "描述你的改动"
git push origin <分支名>

    尽量不要强制添加被忽略的文件

    假设你的 .gitignore 里屏蔽了 .o 文件，但是仍然执行：

    Bash
    git add -f main.o

    会导致强制添加，并把 main.o 当成已追踪文件，所以尽量不要写 -f。

  5. 回到 GitHub 上你的 fork 页面，点击 Contribute → Open pull request。

  6. 写清楚你改了什么、为什么改（详细一点）——一份好的描述会说明：解决了什么问题、怎么解决的、如何测试。记得关联对应的 Issue（比如在描述里写 fixes #12），然后点 Create pull request。
  7. 等待原仓库维护者 review（审查）；他们可能会提意见，你继续修改并 push 即可更新同一个 PR。

补充：

  • 如果只是发现 bug 或提建议，可以直接在仓库的 Issues 页面提交 New issue，这也是贡献的一种方式——怎么写好一份 Issue 见 用 Issue 反馈问题。
  • 如果原仓库给了你写权限，可以跳过 fork，直接建分支改完提 PR。
  • 刚开始接触开源？可以搜索带有 good first issue 标签的 Issue——维护者用它来标记适合新手入门的任务。
  • Pull Request 尽量小而聚焦——一个 PR 解决一个问题，这样更容易被 review 和合并。
  • 还没做完？可以先开 Draft PR（草稿 PR），让维护者知道暂时不要 review。
  • PR 合并之后，你的功能分支就可以放心删除了。

  • 如果原仓库一直在更新，记得不时同步你的 fork：

    Bash
    git remote add upstream https://github.com/原作者/仓库名.git
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

docs.title: 如何创建一个仓库
docs.text:
仓库（Repository） 是项目文件在 GitHub 上的"家"，也是代码托管与协作的基本单位。每个项目都从创建仓库开始。

  1. 登录 github.com，点击右上角的 + 图标，选择 New repository（新建仓库）。
  2. 填写信息：
  3. Repository name（仓库名）：必填，例如 my-first-project。
  4. Description（描述）：可选，简单说明这个仓库是干什么的。
  5. Public / Private：公开仓库任何人都能看；私有仓库只有自己和被邀请的人能看。
  6. Add a README file：建议勾选，自动生成一个 README.md。
  7. Add .gitignore：可选，根据你用的语言（C/C++、Python 等）忽略不需要上传的文件。
  8. Choose a license：可选，选择开源许可证（见 选择许可证）。
  9. 点击 Create repository 完成创建。

命名与可见性

  • 仓库名建议只用小写字母、数字和连字符（例如 my-first-project），这样链接更整洁。
  • Public / Private 之后可以随时在 Settings → General 里修改，现在不必纠结。
  • .gitignore 告诉 Git 哪些文件不需要跟踪（编译产物、IDE 配置文件、密钥等），创建仓库时可以直接套用 GitHub 提供的语言模板。

改名与默认分支

  • 之后可以在 Settings → General 里给仓库改名，但改名后旧链接对所有人都会失效（GitHub 会自动跳转，但别人书签里的链接会受影响），所以尽量在有人引用之前确定好名字。
  • 从 2020 年 10 月起，新仓库的默认分支名是 main（一些老教程里可能还写着 master）。

docs.title: 把代码放进仓库
docs.text:
创建之后，你有两种方式往仓库里放代码：

  • 网页操作：点 Add file → Upload files 直接拖拽上传。
  • 本地 Git：复制仓库地址，在终端执行：
Bash
git clone https://github.com/你的用户名/仓库名.git
# 放入文件后
git add .
git commit -m "first commit"
git push

初次使用 Git 的配置

如果你的电脑还没有配置过用户名和邮箱，就无法提交（commit）。请按下面配置（如果你不想全局配置、只想配置这一个仓库，去掉 --global）：

Bash
git config --global user.name <你的名字，自己想一个>
git config --global user.email <邮箱>
git config --list # 用于确认你的配置状态

docs.title: 如何快速编辑一个仓库里的内容
docs.text:
不需要本地 Git，直接在网页上就能快速改：

  1. 打开仓库里的某个文件，点击右上角的铅笔图标（Edit this file）。
  2. 在编辑框里直接修改内容。
  3. 滚动到页面底部，写一句简短的提交说明（Commit message），选择提交到当前分支或新分支。
  4. 点 Commit changes 保存。

其他网页快捷操作：

  • 新建文件：Add file → Create new file。
  • 上传文件：Add file → Upload files。
  • 删除文件：打开文件 → 右上角垃圾桶图标 → Commit。

Note

网页编辑适合小改动（改个文档、修一行代码）。如果是大改动、需要本地编译测试，还是用 通过 Pull Request 参与贡献里的本地 Git 流程更合适。

更快的办法：网页版编辑器

在任意仓库页面按下键盘上的 .（英文句号），就会在浏览器中打开 github.dev——一个运行在浏览器里的完整 VS Code 编辑器，不用克隆就能浏览、编辑代码，非常方便。

编辑的同时直接发起 PR

网页编辑提交时，可以选择 Create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request——GitHub 会直接帮你创建分支并打开一个 Pull Request。给别人仓库提小修复时，这是非常常用的方式。

docs.title: 如何 Fork 一个仓库
docs.text:
Fork（分叉） 就是把别人的仓库完整复制一份到你自己的账号下，之后你可以自由修改，而不会影响原仓库。

  1. 打开你想 fork 的仓库页面。
  2. 点击右上角的 Fork 按钮（一般在 Star 旁边）。
  3. 选择目标账号（通常就是你自己），点击 Create fork。
  4. 完成后，你账号下就会出现一份同名仓库，标注了 "forked from 原作者/原仓库"。

拿到 fork 后，把它克隆到本地：

Bash
git clone https://github.com/你的用户名/仓库名.git

Fork 与 clone 的区别

Fork 发生在 GitHub 上：整个仓库被复制到你自己的账号下，成为一个新的远端仓库；而 git clone 是把仓库下载到你的本地电脑。要在一个 fork 上开发，通常是两者都做：先 fork，再克隆你自己的 fork。

每个仓库页面上三个按钮的快速对比：

按钮 作用 典型用途 Star ⭐ 把仓库收藏到自己的列表 标记"以后再看"，也是对作者的肯定 Watch 👁 订阅仓库的动态通知 关注项目的新版本和讨论 Fork 把仓库复制到自己账号下 修改代码或准备提 Pull Request

用途：想在别人项目基础上二次开发、学习源码、或者准备给原项目提 Pull Request（见 通过 Pull Request 参与贡献）。如果打算给原项目提交修复，建议先开 Issue 沟通——见 用 Issue 反馈问题。

Fork 不会自动跟随原仓库更新

你的 fork 只是 fork 那一刻的快照。原仓库更新后，你的 fork 不会自动同步——如何通过 upstream 同步见 通过 Pull Request 参与贡献。另外，公开仓库任何人都可以随意 fork，而私有仓库不能被别人 fork。

docs.title: 用 GitHub Pages 发布网页
怎么用 GitHub Pages 发布网页
docs.text:
GitHub Pages 可以把仓库变成一个免费托管的静态网站。

  1. 打开仓库 → Settings → 左侧 Pages。
  2. 在 Build and deployment 下，Source 选择 Deploy from a branch。
  3. 选择分支（通常选 main）和目录（根目录 / 或 /docs），点 Save。
  4. 等几十秒，页面会给出你的网址：https://你的用户名.github.io/仓库名/。

内容来源：

  • 最简单的做法：在仓库根目录放一个 index.html，这就是首页。
  • 也可以使用 Jekyll（GitHub 内置支持）来自动生成博客风格的页面，选一个主题即可。
  • 还有一种"用户主页"型：创建名为 你的用户名.github.io 的仓库，网址就是 https://你的用户名.github.io/。

Tip

如果你不想纯手写 HTML，还可以用 MkDocs（本 workshop 网站就是用 MkDocs 搭建的）或 Hugo 等工具从 Markdown 生成静态网站，再同样发布到 GitHub Pages 上。

常见问题：

  • 第一次部署大约需要一分钟，可以在仓库的 Actions 标签页查看进度。
  • 如果网站返回 404，检查 Source 是否选了 Deploy from a branch，以及所选分支和目录是否正确。
  • 之后向所选分支推送新提交，GitHub Pages 会自动重新构建网站。

两个要知道的点

  • 只能用于公开仓库：免费账号只能从公开仓库发布 Pages（私有仓库需要 GitHub Pro）。
  • 自定义域名：在 Settings → Pages 里可以绑定你自己的域名，GitHub 还会自动签发免费的 HTTPS 证书。

docs.title: Issue 怎么用
docs.text:
Issue 是 GitHub 内置的"工单系统"。任何人都可以用它来：

  • 报告 bug；
  • 提出功能请求；
  • 提问；
  • 记录任务（有些团队甚至用 Issue 规划整个项目）。

Issue 不是给维护者发的私信：它是公开的、可被搜索的，并且会成为仓库历史的一部分——所以认真写好它很重要。

给别人项目写代码之前，也推荐先开一个 Issue：先沟通，再动手（见 通过 Pull Request 参与贡献）。

docs.title: 如何新建一个 Issue
docs.text:
1. 打开仓库，进入 Issues 标签页，点击 New issue。
  2. 如果仓库提供了 Issue 模板（例如 "Bug report"、"Feature request"），选择对应的模板——它会引导你填写。
  3. 写一个清晰的标题，概括问题，例如 在 Windows 上打开 .png 文件时应用崩溃。
  4. 详细描述问题（见下面的清单），然后点击 Submit new issue。

docs.title: 一份好的 Issue 长什么样
docs.text:
• 先搜索：你的问题可能已经有人报告过——在已有的 Issue 下补充评论，而不是重复发一个新的。
  • 一个问题一个 Issue：不要把几个不相关的问题混在一起。
  • 标题清晰：只看标题，维护者就应该知道这大概是什么问题。
  • 复现步骤：一步步说明你做了什么，发生了什么。
  • 预期与实际行为：你期望发生什么，实际发生了什么。
  • 环境信息：操作系统、软件版本、语言版本等。
  • 证据：截图、报错信息或日志片段（日志用代码块包裹）。

docs.title: 一个 Issue 的一生
docs.text:
• 标签（Labels）：维护者会用 bug、enhancement、question、good first issue（适合新手的任务，见 通过 Pull Request 参与贡献）等标签标记 Issue。
  • @ 提醒：在 Issue 正文里写 @用户名 可以提醒特定的人。
  • 关闭（Close）：问题解决后由维护者关闭。如果提交或 PR 的描述里包含 fixes #<Issue 编号>，合并后 GitHub 会自动关闭对应的 Issue。
  • 讨论区（Discussions）：有些项目更喜欢用 GitHub Discussions 进行问答——提问前先看看仓库有没有 Discussions 标签页。

Tip

写一份高质量的 Issue 本身就是对开源的贡献：它同时帮助了维护者和其他使用者。不要害怕报告问题——只要认真描述清楚就好。

docs.title: 实践环节
docs.text:
1. 在自己的仓库里开一个 Issue（比如描述一个你打算加的功能），再自己把它关掉。
  2. 去一个你常用的仓库，找一个带 good first issue 标签的 Issue 读一读，想想自己能不能解决。

docs.title: 什么是许可证（License）
docs.text:
License（许可证） 是一份法律声明，规定别人可以怎样使用你的代码。它是开源项目里很重要的一部分：

许可证 特点 适用场景 MIT 最宽松，别人可以随便用、改、商用，只需保留版权声明 大多数个人项目 Apache 2.0 宽松 + 明确专利授权 企业、需要专利保护 GPL "传染性"强，用了它就必须同样开源 希望衍生项目也开源 BSD 类似 MIT，条款略多 学术类项目 Unlicense 放弃所有权利，代码进入公有领域 希望代码完全无限制使用

要点：

  • 没有 license 是默认"保留所有权利"，别人不能合法地复制或修改你的代码。
  • 添加方法：创建仓库时直接选择，或之后点 Add file → Create new file，把文件名写成 LICENSE.txt，GitHub 会自动提供模板选择。
  • GitHub 按模板生成许可证文件时，会带一行占位的版权信息（[year] [fullname]），记得把它替换成你自己的名字和当前年份。

Tip

不知道选哪个？choosealicense.com 由 GitHub 维护，回答几个简单问题就能帮你推荐一个合适的许可证。

该怎么选？

拿不准的话：个人项目和课程作业选 MIT；在意专利权选 Apache 2.0；希望衍生项目也保持开源选 GPL。许可证之后也可以换——直接替换 LICENSE 文件即可（正规项目里如果有很多贡献者，换之前需要所有贡献者同意）。

docs.title: 怎么编写 README
docs.text:
README.md 是仓库打开后默认展示在首页的说明文档，用 Markdown 编写。它是别人了解你项目的"第一张名片"。

一份好的 README 通常包含：

  • 项目简介：一句话说明这个项目是做什么的。
  • 安装方法：环境依赖、如何安装。
  • 使用方法：怎么运行、示例代码。
  • 许可证 / 贡献方式：指向 LICENSE 或说明如何参与。

docs.title: 常用 Markdown 语法
docs.text:
Markdown
# 一级标题
## 二级标题
- 列表项
**加粗**、*斜体*
`行内代码`
[链接文字](网址)
![图片描述](图片地址)
```
代码块
```

还有一些常用的写法：

Markdown
| 表头 | 表头 |
| --- | --- |
| 单元格 | 单元格 |

- [x] 已完成任务
- [ ] 待办任务

> 引用

创建方法：新建仓库时勾选 "Add a README file"，或之后点 Add file → Create new file，文件名写 README.md。

docs.title: 一个简单的 README 模板
docs.text:
可以从下面这个大纲开始，填入你自己的内容：

Markdown
# 项目名称

一句话说明：这个项目是做什么的？

## 安装方法

如何安装依赖、完成配置。

## 使用方法

如何运行，附上示例命令。

## 参与贡献

其他人可以怎样参与，以及许可证链接。

  • 用 shields.io 生成一行状态徽章（构建状态、许可证、下载量……），会让 README 看起来更专业。
